file_roles.evidence: The unconditional claim is here, 'Settable_routine_parameter *get_settable_routine_parameter() { return this; }', and it becomes '{ return m_is_settable_routine_parameter ? this : NULL; }' with a new private 'bool m_is_settable_routine_parameter'. The commit names this as the change, that the method 'previously always returned this'.

The flag the new branch reads is maintained here: initialised 'm_is_settable_routine_parameter(true)' in the constructor, taken from the bound item in set_from_item with 'm_is_settable_routine_parameter= item->get_settable_routine_parameter()', and cleared in set_default and set_ignore. Without this the header's test has nothing truthful to read.

rationale: The crash is an assertion, 'sql/protocol.cc:1326: virtual Protocol_text::send_out_parameters(List<Item_param>*): Assertion `0' failed', and protocol.cc is not in the gold set. That assertion was correct and was doing its job: the commit explains that it 'guarded that the actual parameter is really settable', and the regression came from MDEV-10709 allowing any expression as an EXECUTE parameter without restricting OUT parameters to settable ones. The caller interrogates the Item_param and the lie is told in the callee.
notes: The file named by every frame and by the assertion text, sql/protocol.cc, is not part of the answer, and the code there needed no change. Worth noting for the benchmark as a whole: this fix spans sql/item.h and sql/item.cc, which are the declaration and definition of one class, so a single logical change counts as two gold files. In C and C++ projects that pairing is routine and inflates gold file counts without adding distinct locations, which is a language-dependent effect on any per-file metric and does not arise in the Java and Scala projects. Worth measuring across the benchmark before reporting per-file numbers.
